title: Rate Limiting
summary: Rate limiting algorithms with internals — Token Bucket, Leaky Bucket, Fixed/Sliding Window — distributed rate limiting, and response headers.

explanation.overview: Rate limiting controls the number of requests a client can make in a time window. It protects your system from abuse (DDoS), ensures fair usage among clients, prevents resource exhaustion, and enforces billing tiers. Every production API has rate limiting — typically implemented at the API Gateway or Load Balancer layer.

key_concepts.definition: INTERNAL: A bucket holds up to C tokens (capacity). Tokens are added at rate R per second. Each request consumes 1 token. If bucket is empty, request is rejected (429 Too Many Requests). IMPLEMENTATION: don't run a timer to add tokens. Instead, compute tokens lazily: on each request, calculate tokens_available = min(C, stored_tokens + R × (now - last_refill_time)). If tokens_available >= 1, allow and decrement. Store: {tokens: float, last_refill: timestamp}. In Redis: two keys per client (tokens + last_refill), updated atomically with a Lua script. BEHAVIOR: allows bursts up to C tokens, then sustains at rate R. Example: C=10, R=2/sec. A client can burst 10 requests instantly, then 2/sec thereafter. CONFIGURABLE: C controls burst size. R controls sustained rate. Different buckets for different endpoints (/api = 100/min, /search = 20/min). USED BY: AWS API Gateway, Stripe, GitHub API.

INTERNAL: requests enter a queue (bucket). The queue drains at a fixed rate R. If the queue is full (capacity C), new requests are dropped. Unlike token bucket, leaky bucket smooths output — no bursts. Output rate is always exactly R, regardless of how bursty the input is. IMPLEMENTATION: use a FIFO queue. A scheduler dequeues and processes at rate R. If queue.size >= C, reject. USE WHEN: you need a perfectly smooth request rate (bandwidth shaping, network traffic policing).

INTERNAL: divide time into fixed windows (60-second intervals). Each window has a counter starting at 0. Each request increments the counter. If counter > limit, reject. At window boundary, counter resets. IMPLEMENTATION (Redis): key = rate_limit:{client_id}:{window_start}. INCR key, EXPIRE key 60. Very simple, O(1) per request. PROBLEM: boundary burst — a client can send limit requests at 00:59 and limit requests at 01:00, effectively getting 2× limit in a 1-second window. FIX: sliding window.

INTERNAL: store the timestamp of every request in a sorted set (Redis ZADD). On each request: remove entries older than window_size ago (ZREMRANGEBYSCORE), count remaining entries (ZCARD), if count < limit, add current timestamp (ZADD). ACCURATE: no boundary issues. EXPENSIVE: stores one entry per request. 1000 requests/minute × 1M users = 1B entries. Too much memory. USE: when accuracy matters and traffic is low.

INTERNAL: combines fixed window with weighted averaging. Keep counters for current window and previous window. Estimated count = prev_window_count × overlap_percentage + curr_window_count. Example: 60-second windows. We're 15 seconds into the current window. Previous window had 45 requests. Current window has 18 requests. Estimated rate = 45 × (45/60) + 18 = 45 × 0.75 + 18 = 33.75 + 18 = 51.75. If limit is 60, allow. IMPLEMENTATION: just two counters (2 Redis keys per client). O(1) memory. Error < 0.003% in practice. USED BY: Cloudflare for their rate limiting. This is the industry-standard algorithm — simple, memory-efficient, and accurate enough.

examples.title: Stripe's 4-Dimensional Rate Limiting Architecture
examples.description: How Stripe, a developer-first financial API, uses multiple concurrent rate limiters to guarantee platform stability without punishing legitimate users.
examples.code:
The Problem:
Stripe processes billions of API calls for payments globally. A simple '100 requests per second' limit per user is insufficient because some operations (like creating a charge) are highly resource-intensive, while others (like retrieving a past transaction) are cheap.

The Architecture (4 Types of Limiters):
Stripe employs four distinct types of rate limiters simultaneously:
1. Request Rate Limiters: The standard API limit (e.g., 100 req/sec per user). Uses a fast Redis Token Bucket.
2. Concurrent Requests Limiters: Prevents resource exhaustion from slow endpoints. If a user tries to run 50 simultaneous heavy 'Search' queries that each take 2 seconds, they are blocked even if their req/sec limit is high.
3. Fleet Usage Limiters: Limits total platform traffic across all users. If Stripe's internal capacity is dwindling during Black Friday, they throttle lower-priority API calls globally to ensure critical payments always process.
4. Worker Utilization Limiters: If a specific backend service (e.g., the Webhook Sender) is overloaded, it sheds load by returning 429s specifically for that service, preserving the rest of the API.

Takeaway for Interviews:
Advanced rate limiting is not just about counting HTTP requests. It's about protecting backend compute, managing concurrency, and prioritizing critical business paths over non-critical ones.

examples.title: Rate Limiting Algorithm Strategy Matrix
examples.description: Evaluate the optimal rate limiting algorithm based on business edge cases.
examples.code:
ALGORITHM                    | MEMORY USE | BURST HANDLING | BOUNDARY ISSUES | BEST USED FOR
-----------------------------|------------|----------------|-----------------|-----------------------------------------------------
Token Bucket                 | Low (O(1)) | Excellent      | No              | General API usage (Stripe, AWS API Gateway)
Leaky Bucket                 | Med (Queue)| None (Smoothed)| No              | Throttling asynchronous background traffic/queues
Fixed Window Counter         | Lowest     | Moderate       | Yes (2x limit)  | Basic quota limits (e.g., 500 emails per day)
Sliding Window Log           | Very High  | Excellent      | No              | Extremely precise limiting for low-volume/high-value APIs
Sliding Window Counter       | Low (O(1)) | Excellent      | No              | High-traffic global edge API limits (Cloudflare)

examples.title: Failure Modes & Exception Handling
examples.description: How to handle catastrophic failures and network partitions in this tier.
examples.code:
try-catch fallback mechanics:
1. NetworkTimeoutException: Trigger circuit breaker and return stale cached data.
2. ConnectionRefusedException: Shift traffic to the standby region (Pilot Light architecture).
3. OOMError: Restart exact instance via Kubernetes Health Probes.

advanced_tweaks.how: Rate limit by: IP address (100 req/min per IP), API key (1000 req/min per key), user ID (50 req/min per user), endpoint (/login has stricter limit). A single request must pass ALL rate limits.

Instead of hard blocking at limit, degrade gradually: 0-80% of limit = full speed. 80-100% = add artificial delay (100-500ms). 100%+ = return 429. This gives the client a chance to back off before being hard-blocked.

key_concepts.definition: All rate limit state in Redis. Every request checks Redis via Lua script (atomic INCR + EXPIRE). PROS: accurate (single source of truth, no over-allowance). CONS: Redis is a SPOF for rate limiting (if Redis is down, do you allow all or deny all?). Added latency (~0.5ms per request). FIX for SPOF: fail open (allow all requests if Redis is down) for most APIs. Fail closed (block all) for critical endpoints (payment, login).

Each app server maintains local rate limit counters. Periodically sync with central store (every 1-5 seconds). Between syncs, each server allows limit/num_servers requests. PROS: no single point of failure, no per-request latency to Redis. CONS: allows slight over-limit (up to num_servers × overage_per_server). Acceptable for most use cases — rate limits are soft boundaries.

Always return rate limit info in response headers: X-RateLimit-Limit: 100 (max requests per window), X-RateLimit-Remaining: 42 (requests left in current window), X-RateLimit-Reset: 1710456789 (Unix timestamp when window resets), Retry-After: 30 (seconds to wait, included with 429 response).

examples.title: Token Bucket Implementation via Redis Lua Scripting
examples.description: A production-grade algorithmic snippet ensuring perfectly atomic distributed rate limiting without CPU loops or race conditions.
examples.code:
-- The Redis KEYs and ARGs provided by the application
local tokens_key = KEYS[1]
local timestamp_key = KEYS[2]

local rate = tonumber(ARGV[1])
local capacity = tonumber(ARGV[2])
local now = tonumber(ARGV[3])
local requested = tonumber(ARGV[4])

-- Fetch current state limit per client
local last_tokens = tonumber(redis.call("get", tokens_key))
if last_tokens == nil then
    last_tokens = capacity
end

local last_refreshed = tonumber(redis.call("get", timestamp_key))
if last_refreshed == nil then
    last_refreshed = 0
end

local delta = math.max(0, now - last_refreshed)
-- Refill based on time elapsed
local filled_tokens = math.min(capacity, last_tokens + (delta * rate))
local allowed = filled_tokens >= requested
local new_tokens = filled_tokens

if allowed then
    -- Consume tokens
    new_tokens = filled_tokens - requested
end

-- Update Redis keys unconditionally
redis.call("setex", tokens_key, 60, new_tokens)
redis.call("setex", timestamp_key, 60, now)

return { allowed, new_tokens }
